extraction.name: Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD)
extraction.description: A reading comprehension dataset consisting of 100,000+ questions posed by crowdworkers on a set of Wikipedia articles, where the answer to each question is a segment of text from the corresponding reading passage.
extraction.creator: Pranav Rajpurkar and Jian Zhang and Konstantin Lopyrev and Percy Liang
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was collected in three stages: curating passages from Wikipedia articles, crowdsourcing question-answer pairs on those passages using Amazon Mechanical Turk, and obtaining additional answers for the development and test sets.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: If a question could not be answered by a span in the paragraph, workers were instructed to submit the question without marking an answer.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data consisted of the top 10,000 articles from English Wikipedia (based on Project Nayuki's internal PageRanks), from which 536 articles were sampled and 23,215 paragraphs were extracted after filtering out images, figures, tables, and short paragraphs.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Crowdworkers were asked to generate up to 5 questions per paragraph and highlight the corresponding answers in the text. They were provided with guidelines, sample paragraphs, and examples of good and bad questions/answers. They were also instructed to use their own words rather than copying from the text.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Daemo platform with Amazon Mechanical Turk backend
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 1 original answer for the training set, and at least 3 answers (1 original + at least 2 additional) for the development and test sets.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Located in the United States or Canada
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is limited to span-based answers, which are more constrained than interpretative questions. Additionally, a small portion of the data (6.1%) contains ambiguous questions or lacks a unique answer.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed for training and evaluating modern, data-intensive machine learning models on reading comprehension tasks.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset is versioned (e.g., v1.0, v1.1) and is freely available online, though specific update timeframes or deprecation policies are not explicitly detailed.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Sampled 536 articles uniformly at random and partitioned them randomly into training (80%), development (10%), and test (10%) sets.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Extracted individual paragraphs, stripped away images, figures, and tables, and discarded paragraphs shorter than 500 characters.

inLanguage.evidence: Consider the question “ what causes precipitation to fall? ” posed on the passage in Figure 1.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: We collect our dataset in three stages: curating passages, crowdsourcing question-answers on those passages, and obtaining additional answers.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: Next, we employed crowdworkers to create questions. We used the Daemo platform (Gaikwad et al., 2015), with Amazon Mechanical Turk as its backend.

rai:dataCollectionMissingData.evidence: If a question was not answerable by a span in the paragraph, workers were asked to submit the question without marking an answer.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: we used Project Nayuki’s Wikipedia’s internal PageRanks to obtain the top 10000 articles of English Wikipedia, from which we sampled 536 articles uniformly at random. From each of these articles, we extracted individual paragraphs, stripping away images, ﬁgures, tables, and discarding paragraphs shorter than 500 characters.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: On each paragraph, crowdworkers were tasked with asking and answering up to 5 questions on the content of that paragraph. The questions had to be entered in a text ﬁeld, and the answers had to be highlighted in the paragraph. To guide the work-ers, tasks contained a sample paragraph, and exam-ples of good and bad questions and answers on that paragraph along with the reasons they were cate-gorized as such.

rai:dataAnnotationPlatform.evidence: We used the Daemo platform (Gaikwad et al., 2015), with Ama-zon Mechanical Turk as its backend.

rai:annotationsPerItem.evidence: we obtained at least 2 additional answers for each question in the develop-ment and test sets.

rai:annotatorDemographics.evidence: Crowdworkers were required to have a 97% HIT acceptance rate, a minimum of 1000 HITs, and be located in the United States or Canada.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: While questions with span-based answers are more constrained than the more interpretative questions found in more advanced standardized tests, we still ﬁnd a rich diversity of questions and answer types in SQuAD. [...] Ambiguous: We don’t agree with the crowdworkers’ answer, or the question does not have a unique answer. (6.1%)
